lessons.title: Safety and handling a horse for grooming
lessons.html:
Safety first

Horses are big, strong animals. A frightened horse can kick, bite, strike or knock you over without meaning to. Most accidents happen when people are careless. Follow these rules every time.

Rules around horses

  • Wear closed boots, preferably with steel toes, and neat clothes.
  • Speak to the horse before you approach so it knows you are there.
  • Approach from the front-left, towards the shoulder, never straight from behind.
  • When you walk around the back, keep a hand on the horse and stay very close, or walk well out of kicking range.
  • Never kneel or sit on the ground near a horse. Squat so you can move away.
  • Never wrap a lead rope around your hand.
  • Watch the horse's ears, eyes and tail. Ears pinned back or a swishing tail can mean the horse is upset.

Putting on a headcollar

  1. Enter the stable calmly and close the door.
  2. Stand at the left shoulder. Put the lead rope over the neck.
  3. Slip the noseband over the nose.
  4. Bring the headpiece over behind the ears and buckle it on the left side.
  5. It should fit snugly: two fingers under the noseband.

Tying up

Tie the horse to a string loop attached to the ring, not directly to the ring. If the horse pulls back hard, the string breaks before the horse gets hurt. Always use a quick-release knot so you can free the horse with one pull. Tie at about the height of the horse's eye, with a rope short enough that it cannot get a leg over.

Moving the horse over

To move the horse over, press gently on its side with your hand where your leg would be and say "over". Praise it when it moves.

Groom in a safe place: a clean, dry area with a non-slip floor, out of the wind, away from busy walkways.

lessons.title: The grooming kit and grooming routine
lessons.html:
The grooming kit

ToolUse
Rubber curry combLoosens dried mud, dead hair and dust in circles; not on bony parts
Dandy brush (stiff)Removes dried mud and dirt; not on the face or clipped areas
Body brush (soft)Removes dust and grease from the coat, mane and tail
Metal curry combCleans the body brush only; never use on the horse
Mane combCombs and tidies the mane
Sponges (2)One for eyes and nose, one for the dock area
Hoof pickCleans out the feet
Stable rubber (cloth)Final polish
Sweat scraperRemoves water after a bath

Caring for the kit

Each horse should have its own kit to stop skin diseases such as ringworm spreading. Knock out brushes after each use. Wash the kit once a week in warm soapy water, rinse, and dry with the bristles facing down. Keep it in a box. Replace worn brushes.

Grooming steps

  1. Tie the horse up safely.
  2. Pick out the feet (see next lesson).
  3. Use the rubber curry comb in small circles over the muscly parts of the body.
  4. Use the dandy brush with short flicks in the direction of the hair to remove loose dirt, on the body and legs.
  5. Use the body brush in long strokes. After every few strokes clean it on the metal curry comb. Tap the curry comb on the floor to empty it.
  6. Brush the face gently with the body brush. Untie the horse first or hold the headcollar.
  7. Brush the mane and tail by hand or with the body brush, a few hairs at a time, to avoid breaking hair.
  8. Sponge the eyes, nose and lips with one sponge; use the other for the dock.
  9. Finish with the stable rubber.

Bathing

Bath on a warm day, out of the wind. Start at the legs so the horse gets used to the water, then the body; avoid the face and ears. Use horse shampoo, rinse well, scrape off water with the sweat scraper, then walk the horse dry or put on a cooler. Never put a wet horse in a cold stable.

While grooming, look for cuts, lumps, heat, ticks and skin problems, and report them.

lessons.title: Cleaning and caring for the hooves
lessons.html:
No foot, no horse

This old saying means a horse with bad feet cannot work. Clean feet every day, before and after work.

Picking up a foreleg

  1. Stand at the horse's left shoulder facing the tail.
  2. Run your hand down the back of the leg to the fetlock.
  3. Squeeze gently and say "up".
  4. When the horse lifts the foot, hold it with your hand under the hoof wall.

For a hind leg, stand close to the hip facing the tail, run your hand down the outside or back of the leg and lift. Keep your body close to the horse, not behind the leg.

Picking out the foot

  1. Use the hoof pick from heel towards toe, away from you.
  2. Clean the grooves on each side of the frog carefully.
  3. Do not dig into the soft frog.
  4. Remove stones, mud and dung.
  5. Put the foot down gently; do not drop it.

Go in the same order every time, for example near fore, near hind, off fore, off hind. Pick out the feet into a skip, not onto clean bedding.

What to check

  • Bad smell and black, sticky matter in the frog grooves (signs of thrush)
  • Stones or nails stuck in the sole
  • Cracks in the hoof wall
  • Loose or twisted shoes and raised nail ends (clenches)
  • Heat in the foot or a strong pulse at the back of the fetlock
  • Lameness when the horse walks

Report any of these to your supervisor. If a nail has gone into the foot, do not pull it out; keep the horse still and call your supervisor so the vet can see where it went in.

Hoof care

Keep stables clean and dry. Wet, dirty bedding causes thrush. Apply hoof oil only if the yard uses it, on clean dry hooves. The farrier visits regularly, usually every few weeks; keep the date on the yard board.

Key points

  • Approach horses calmly from the front-left and never kneel near them.
  • Tie up to a string loop with a quick-release knot.
  • Each horse has its own clean grooming kit.
  • Curry comb, dandy brush, body brush, sponges, then stable rubber.
  • Pick out feet daily from heel to toe and report thrush, stones, cracks and loose shoes.
